rationale: B wins because it turns the hardest fact into the story instead of hiding it: "The refusal to split cuts from unfilled roles is part of the story, not a footnote." A has real material, but "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" commits the sin it later warns against: it treats a chat-resolution metric as a dispute-outcome fact. That is the difference between an angle a reporter can stress-test and a line someone will have to walk back.
gaps_in_A: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is not supported. The update gives average customer-service chat resolution time, not dispute resolution time or dispute accuracy.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is plausible color dressed as fact. The update does not establish comparative rarity.

"Klarna is profitable, has filed to go public, and is leading with an AI-efficiency story" overstates the filing. The update says it filed to go public; it does not say the filing leads with AI efficiency.

The data and labor angles lean on the same 700-FTE/headcount material. Both can live, but the first angle needs a cleaner operational-metrics protagonist instead of bleeding into AI-displacement coverage.
gaps_in_B: "a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" still leans past the facts. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that the assistant rules on charge outcomes.
"AI-shrunk cost base" assumes a cost-base result the update does not give. Headcount fell and resolution time improved; cost structure needs filing or P&L proof.
"whether any of the displaced work was outsourced rather than in-house" is a fair reporter question, but it appears from nowhere. Keep it framed as a pure unknown, not a hinted fact.
"Next step: `meanest-editor`" is the wrong handoff for an angle set. Pick the angle, close the proof gap, then do journalist fit before drafting.
